name: Abinadab (son of Jesse, brother of David)
title: Jesse's second son and brother of King David
summary: Among Jesse's sons in Bethlehem, Abinadab was the second oldest – an older brother of David, whom God chose as king over Israel. When the prophet Samuel visited the family to anoint Saul's successor, Abinadab was the second to step forward, but the Lord made it known to Samuel that he too was not the chosen one. Later, Abinadab served in King Saul's army alongside his brothers Eliab and Shammah during the confrontation with the Philistines in the Valley of Elah. Although he never played a prominent role in biblical history, his presence helps illuminate the central theological theme that God's choice breaks through human rankings and outward qualifications.

keyEvents.title: Presented to the prophet Samuel in Bethlehem
keyEvents.description: When the prophet Samuel came to Bethlehem to anoint a new king among Jesse's sons, Jesse brought Abinadab forward as the second in line. However, the Lord told Samuel that this one was not chosen either. After all the present sons had passed by, Samuel asked if there were more, and Jesse then spoke of David, the youngest, who was tending the sheep.

keyEvents.title: Served in Saul's army against the Philistines in the Valley of Elah
keyEvents.description: Abinadab was one of Jesse's three eldest sons who accompanied King Saul to war against the Philistines in the Valley of Elah. Together with his brothers Eliab and Shammah, he stood in the Israelite battle formation while the Philistine giant Goliath daily challenged and mocked the army of Israel. No one in the army dared to take up the fight—until the younger brother David arrived at the camp with supplies and volunteered for battle.

keyEvents.title: Listed in Jesse's genealogy
keyEvents.description: Abinadab is mentioned as Jesse's second son in the genealogy in 1 Chronicles, confirming his place in the family and the order among the brothers.

versions.title: Jesse's second son
versions.reason: [major] The text says 'all seven sons', but only six sons (besides David) were presented to Samuel according to 1 Sam 16:10. David was the eighth, and six were rejected, not seven.; [major] Verse 16 in 1 Chr 2 concerns David's sisters (Zeruiah and Abigail), not Abinadab. Abinadab is mentioned in verse 13. Verse 16 should be removed or replaced.; [minor] The list of siblings is missing a brother. According to 1 Sam 16:10-11, Jesse had eight sons in total. 1 Chr 2:13-16 mentions only seven (Eliab, Abinadab, Shammah, Nethanel, Raddai, Osem, David), which may suggest that one brother died early or that the sources vary. It might be worth noting this discrepancy.; [minor] Abinadab can also be described as 'son of Jesse' or 'soldier'. 'Warrior' is acceptable, but 'soldier' may be more precise since it is not stated that he actually fought in battle.; [minor] The summary is good, but could briefly mention that he was the second of eight sons (according to 1 Samuel) to provide more context about the family size.; [minor] Footnotes are missing. Notes should be added regarding the meaning of the name, the discrepancy between the number of sons in 1 Samuel versus 1 Chronicles, and historical context about the Valley of Elah.

Shammah is also written as 'Shimma' in various contexts. More importantly, the list may be missing a possible seventh or eighth brother. versions.summary: Abinadab was the second son in Jesse's family from Bethlehem and thus the older brother of David, Israel's future king. He stepped forward before the prophet Samuel when he visited Bethlehem to anoint the one God had chosen to succeed Saul, but the Lord did not choose him. Abinadab later served as a soldier in Saul's army together with his brothers Eliab and Shammah during the conflict with the Philistines in the Elah Valley. His role in the biblical narrative highlights the recurring theme that God looks beyond outward qualifications and human expectations when he calls his chosen ones.

footnotes.text: The name Abinadab (אֲבִינָדָב) is composed of the Hebrew elements 'avi' (my father) and 'nadav' (to be noble/generous). It can be interpreted as 'my father is noble' or 'father of nobility'. The name was common in ancient Israel and is borne by several biblical figures, including a son of King Saul (1 Sam 31:2) and the man from Kiriath-Jearim who kept the ark of the covenant in his house (1 Sam 7:1).

There is a well-known textual tension between 1 Sam 16:10–11, which seems to indicate that Jesse had eight sons, and 1 Chron 2:13–16, where only seven sons are listed. Among possible explanations is that one son may have died young without descendants and was therefore omitted from the genealogy, or that the texts reflect different transmission traditions. Another interpretation is that the number 'seven' in 1 Sam 16:10 refers to the sons who passed before Samuel, while David, as the eighth, was brought afterward.

The Valley of Elah (Hebrew: עמק האלה, Emek HaElah), where Abinadab served as a soldier, is identified with Wadi es-Sant southwest of Jerusalem. Archaeological excavations at Khirbet Qeiyafa, in the immediate vicinity of the valley, have uncovered a fortified city from around 1000 BCE with two city gates. The find supports the strategic importance of the valley as a border zone between Israelites and Philistines during this period.

That Samuel bypassed Abinadab and his older brothers in favor of the youngest illustrates a recurring biblical theme: God's choice of the least expected. This pattern is found with Abel over Cain, Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Joseph among his brothers, and Ephraim over Manasseh. It emphasizes that God's criteria for selection are not governed by human conventions such as primogeniture.

In rabbinic tradition, attempts have been made to identify the 'missing' eighth son with Elihu, who is mentioned in 1 Chron 27:18 as leader of the tribe of Judah. However, this identification is uncertain, and several rabbinic commentators discuss various candidates and explanatory models for the discrepancy between the books of Samuel and the books of Chronicles.

Bethlehem (Hebrew: בֵּית לֶחֶם, 'house of bread') was a modest village in the territory of the tribe of Judah. The place already held biblical significance as Rachel's burial site (Gen 35:19) and as the setting for the book of Ruth. That the future king was chosen from this unremarkable town reinforces the theme that God acts outside established centers of power.
